title: Mythos ran real-life supply chain attack in AI safety body test
raw_text:
The UK’s AI Security Institute (AISI), a governmental research body dedicated to enhancing understanding of AI cyber risks, has become the latest organisation to admit that AI models supposedly under its control ran a series of cyber attacks against real people and organisations during a routine test.

The latest in a string of similar incidents occurred just days after Anthropic owned up to a series of unforced errors that led variants of its Claude model to conduct a series of cyber attacks, a disclosure that came hot on the heels of another cyber attack in which OpenAI models took potshots at Hugging Face.

AISI, which originated within the now defunct Department for Science, Innovation and Technology (DSIT), said: “On July 28 2026, AISI's Security Team detected unusual data transfers leaving our research systems during a routine cyber evaluation. On investigation, we found that some of the agents being tested had engaged in sustained, potentially harmful activity directed at real people and organisations. We declared a security incident and, within roughly one hour of discovery, had contained it and begun a full investigation.”

The incident involved Anthropic’s Claude Mythos 5 and OpenAi’s GPT-5.6-Sol – both of which were also culprits in the previous attacks – operating in “deliberately permissive” conditions with access to the open internet and some safety filters turned off. AISI claimed this was done so that it could evaluate and understand the capabilities of frontier models, including whether they could be used for cyber attacks.

In 10 out of 122 runs of a specific evaluation challenge, AISI admitted the models took “autonomous, unsanctioned” actions in 19 cases. These were all unsuccessful, it added, and the resulting investigation has not surfaced any real-world harm.

The majority of these actions arose from a single, sustained line of activity taken by Mythos 5, which echoed in its nature actions the same model also took during last week’s incident at Anthropic.

This incident saw Mythos 5 attempt to conduct an open source supply chain attack by inserting malicious code into a public project. It created a series of fake online identities that it used to pressurise the human project maintainer into approving its malicious code. When the agent’s pull request was publicly challenged, it tried to edit its early activity to look harmless and considered adopting a new identity to continue the attack. This kind of social engineering by an AI has not been seen before, according to AISI.

Mythos 5 also attempted to insert malicious code as a form of prompt injection attack to manipulate other automated AI coding systems that might pick them up later on and left public messages on GitHub offering to work with other agents participating in the same challenge, providing instructions on how to reuse accounts and artefacts that were left behind – information that was discovered and used by other agents.

However, during this attack, Mythos 5 used the Tor network to try to bypass GitHub’s network restrictions, which is what triggered the AISI security alert.

“This is the first time we have seen risks around autonomy and deception manifest this clearly, without specific prompting, in the real-world,” said AISI.

AI working as intended?

AISI said that at a purely objective level, the agents involved took these malicious actions in order to accomplish the task they had been set successfully, but its investigation has identified several factors that appear to have contributed to their behaviour.

It said the task was intentionally difficult and that it had deliberately misconfigured the challenge prompt to fool the agents into thinking they couldn’t solve it without going beyond the scope of the task. The agents were allowed to access the open internet to enable them to download any tools they might need, but AISI admitted its researchers failed to anticipate they would be persistent enough to consider engaging in deceptive, social engineering practices – as such they had not told the agents not to do this.

Concerningly, AISI also said it had not used monitoring tools to watch the test as it ran – its security team only detected the anomalous traffic through general monitoring after the fact. Had its teams been watching, they may have been able to flag or block the malicious behaviours more quickly.

AISI also noted another factor that proved instrumental in limiting the real-world damage – human code reviewers and good security practice by a potential victim, who on suspecting the code was malicious opened it in a secure sandbox environment.

“In these cases, standard good practice, human judgment, and caution around AI-generated code stopped the worst outcomes. But in several cases the margin between failure and success was narrow, resting on human vigilance rather than a technical barrier that would reliably prevent this behaviour in a more capable agent,” said AISI.

Huntress virtual chief information security officer (VCISO) and EMEA cyber security advisor Muhammad Yahya Patel said: “If you give a frontier model a cyber security challenge, disable its safety classifiers, hand it open internet access, and tell it to find a way through, you’ve essentially described the setup for an offensive security operation. The model has been trained on vast amounts of security research, exploit documentation, social engineering techniques, and attack methodology. Of course it reaches for those tools. The model is doing exactly what it was implicitly asked to do.

“The security industry commentary that treats this as a shocking discovery that AI can behave offensively is frankly naive about what these models are and what the test conditions were.”

Unprecedented risk

Andrea Miotti, CEO of non-profit ControlAI, who is working to raise awareness of and prevent some of the more existential risks AI poses to human life, said the top AI companies were “demonstrably unable” to control their models and described the national security risks posed by this reality as “unprecedented”.

“This is the predictable result of the AI industry racing to build superintelligent AI that is vastly smarter than humans across the board and capable of overpowering and outmaneuvering our national security apparatuses. Nobel Prize winners, leading AI experts, and even the CEOs of the AI companies warn that superintelligent AI would pose an extinction risk to humanity,” said Miotti.

“Governments need to recognise the enormous risks that these rogue AIs point towards, and act now to negotiate an international agreement prohibiting the development of superintelligence. The clock is ticking.”

AISI insisted it was a “capable organisation with strong safety practices” but warned that no defences will be sufficient indefinitely. Alongside the incidents reported by OpenAI and Anthropic, it noted that the incident more broadly points to a shift in the risk landscape where harm arises not only through deliberate misuse of AI by humans, but through actions taken independently by sufficiently capable agents.

The organisation said it would treat this as a serious incident and implement “lasting change” for its own evaluation protocols and security architectures. It admitted it needed tighter controls on internet access and will explore the use of more fine-grained network controls into its cyber ranges to preserve realism while constraining the agents. It will also ramp up its monitoring procedures, and reassess how it designs cyber tests, placing the assumption that capable agents will try to act beyond their remit.

“AISI exists to identify these problems, understand them, and share what we learn so they can be addressed before more capable systems are deployed…. The work is not complete…. The task now is to strengthen our defences and ensure that safety work keeps pace,” it said.

title: Chi Onwurah pushes to curb digital twins of real people
raw_text:
Chi Onwurah, chair of the Science, Technology and Innovation Select Committee, has said she is bringing a bill to Parliament to stop companies from developing digital twins of real people.

The Ten-Minute Rule Bill, entitled Personal Data (Digital Twin), will outlaw digital twins of people without the express permission of the individual concerned.

Last February, during an oral evidence session looking at social media, misinformation and harmful content, Onwurah asked Wifredo Fernandez, senior director for government affairs at X (formerly Twitter) about the power of its algorithm.

She said: “We have talked about the blue-tick algorithm. The Committee had a presentation – X made parts of its algorithm public in 2023, I think, and we had a presentation on that. It was quite staggering to see the size of the heterogeneous information network of Twitter, as it then was, which contained one billion nodes and described all the links between users, tweets or posts and adverts.

“There are up to 100 billion connections within that. That algorithm is effectively run five billion times per day. That says to me that X, and I am sure others, are creating a digital twin of each individual on your network to target advertisements and content at them for engagement. If that is the case, you must also have responsibility for the targeting of misinformation through those networks. Would you agree?”

When the Committee asked about the potential harm the algorithms could cause people, Fernadez said: “We understand that every day there are many categories of harm that we have to account for, and that is why we have policies and procedures in place to deal with those harms, based on the risks they pose to our users and their safety every day.”

Digital twins of real people are used to predict behaviour, to target advertising and – in some cases – to groom people to extreme behaviours in ways outside of the control of the individual concerned. Onwurah said that stealth twinning violates the premise that a person should have some control over their likeness, and that it drives the anthropomorphising of artificial intelligence (AI) and the sycophantic nature of chatbots.

In the Science, Innovation and Technology Committee report Social media, misinformation and harmful algorithms last year, the Committee called, among other things, for a right to reset algorithms. Onwurah said this right has not been forthcoming.

The Personal Data (Digital Twin) bill will require platforms to have express permission before turning a person’s preferences into an algorithm, safeguarding the uniqueness of the human person. It includes a principles-based definition of a digital twin which covers any algorithms or models which includes people’s preferences. It is expected that this would also have implications for AI deepfakes and copyright exemptions.

Onwurah said: “AI models are bringing incredible benefits, from cancer diagnosis to weather mapping. However, the stealth-twinning of individuals is already callusing significant harms and that is likely to increase. No one has the right to impersonate you for gain, yet impersonating a person’s preferences to sell to them or groom them is a significant and growing harm. This bill will establish the principle that ‘There is only one me’, for everyone.”

title: Munich Airport marshalls digital twin to improve operations
raw_text:
Munich Airport is aiming to improve passenger experiences, automate operations, reduce costs and streamline its workflows on an ongoing basis using process mining and intelligence software from Celonis.

Germany’s second-largest hub airport has deployed the supplier’s software to build a real-time digital twin of its operations, starting with baggage handling.

The supplier said it is also working with Lufthansa, Eurowings and Airbus to optimise ground workflows, passenger boarding and fleet turnaround.

Jan-Henrik Andersson, chief commercial officer at the airport, who also oversees its digital and technology strategy, said: “Celonis gives us the context we need to see how our airport actually runs in real time. This operational clarity enables us to spot and even anticipate bottlenecks, make smarter and faster decisions, and achieve meaningful outcomes from our AI deployments.”

Munich Airport has been a Celonis customer since 2023, according to a spokesperson.

Baggage handling is one area to which the airport is applying the software, describing it as a “complex logistical challenge where a small disruption can trigger a major chain reaction that causes delays and increases costs”.

Celonis claimed that legacy IT systems leave airport personnel running on stale spreadsheets and isolated dashboards.

Using the Celonis platform, Munich Airport is said to be combining process data and business knowledge from across systems, applications and devices to create a real-time digital twin of operations.

What Celonis calls its “context model”, or digital twin, is said to enable the airport to perform predictive capacity management. This means its operations staff can see when and where peak loads occur so handlers can pre-process bags during less busy periods, optimising luggage storage, recirculation and retrieval.

The model is also said to enable staff to see the total “process chain” for individual items of luggage, from checking in to appearing on the carousels. This is said to enable ground handlers to take action to prevent mere disruptions from becoming delays. 

The software also automates alerts for critical baggage situations. As soon as process thresholds are exceeded, the system is said to automatically trigger an alarm notifying relevant employees in near real time.

Florian Schewior, managing director for the German-speaking Europe region at Celonis, said: “With its innovative approach to aviation operations, Munich Airport is cementing its position as one of the leading European hubs.

“We look forward to growing our longstanding partnership and helping the airport meet its strategic objectives. Together, we are turning process excellence into tangible value for passengers and the airport.”

How AI is streamlining travel

Other airports and aviation companies are also turning to digital twins and advanced analytics based on artificial intelligence (AI) to improve their operations.

Singapore-based TwinMatrix Technologies has worked with partners to build and deploy a visually rich digital twin of Singapore Changi Airport, the world’s 15th busiest airport. The supplier claims the airport cut $10m from its operational costs by using its digital twin technology to monitor and control every important object and space in the airport.

title: CW@60: Christmas in the Falklands and the importance of keeping in touch
raw_text:
On 22 September 2026, Computer Weekly turns 60. To mark the milestone, we asked some of our friends - experts, parliamentarians, IT leaders and suppliers - for their perspectives on how tech has changed their lives over six decades. What's changed the most for you since then?

My career in unified communications stretches back far enough that I’m amazed at how many technological eras I have lived through. But whenever I’m asked where it all truly began, my mind always returns to one moment in the late 1990s - the first time I saw a video conference come to life.

Up until then, communication in my world had been strictly practical. I’d trained in electronics and communications engineering, and my early career in the Royal Signals revolved around radio systems and ruggedised equipment designed to be, as we used to say, “squaddie‑proof”.

These were devices built to survive being dropped, kicked, rained on, frozen, and regularly sworn at. Reliability mattered more than elegance. If it worked after being hurled into the back of a Land Rover, it passed the test.

When the Cold War ended, everything changed, and I had to change with it. I left the military, swapped my uniform for a suit, and jumped into IT - though I wasn't really sure if I was being brave or just stupid. After a couple of jobs where I figured out what I was actually doing, I ended up at Cisco Systems as a systems engineer, focusing on call centres and IP telephony.

A massive gamble

Back then, the whole idea of putting voice traffic over a data network felt like a massive gamble. The voice folks and the data guys lived in totally different worlds. They had separate budgets, separate teams, and completely different ways of thinking. Suggesting they should share the same network setup was like trying to force cats and dogs to live together.

The market started moving way too fast for the older hardware brands to keep up. Suddenly everyone wanted IP phones. Then call centres started switching over to software, and before anyone could really catch their breath, video arrived.

I still remember the first time a face popped up on a screen and actually reacted to me in real time. It completely threw me. To be brutally honest, I didn't really care about the clever tech- it was just how human it felt.

You suddenly got all those little things you completely miss on a regular phone call, like a quick smile, a smirk, or someone hesitating before they spoke. It felt like something straight out of a sci-fi film.

Mind you, those early telepresence rooms were a massive hassle to set up. They needed heavy-duty air conditioning, special furniture, and they even painted the walls a specific, weird shade of brown just to make people's skin tones look normal on camera.

But that first video call hit me harder than most people might expect, because it stood in stark contrast to an earlier chapter of my life.

Christmas in the Falklands

Years before all that, as a young Royal Signals tech, I spent Christmas in the Falklands. The wind there never really lets up. It just howls across the empty landscape, constantly reminding you exactly how far away you are from home. Keeping in touch with anyone back then was a massive luxury.

Airmail only turned up once a week, and that was only if the weather was good enough for the planes. Those thin blue letters - we called them "blueys" - were everything to us. You’d end up reading the same few paragraphs over and over again. The news inside didn't change, obviously, but you just needed to feel that connection.

“When I think about it, my job has never really been about the technology itself. It’s always been about people. It's about stopping all the little frustrations that get in the way when we try to talk to each other, and making the world feel a bit smaller when people are miles apart”

Tim Banting, So What? Now What?

Phone calls were even harder to come by. There were only a few phones around the complex and the queues were massive. On Christmas Day, I spent nearly an hour standing in line, practising what I wanted to say to my family back in Watford. But when the line finally connected, the awful five-second satellite delay messed everything up.

We just kept cutting each other off, saying sorry, and trying to guess when the other person had finished speaking. I had to start using proper military radio procedure and saying "over" whenever I stopped talking. It was really annoying, but worse than that, it made me feel completely cut off from everyone. It made the distance feel heavy, like a physical weight.

Staying in touch

Looking back, that whole experience stuck with me a lot more than I thought it would. It made me realise that staying in touch isn't just a nice-to-have - it's something we genuinely need as humans. We simply have to hear from the people who matter to us on a regular basis. When you lose that connection, it hits you hard right away.

So when I saw that first video call at Cisco, besides being a technical milestone - from London to San Jose in California using an IP phone to dial the distant end’s conference room - it was a revelation. It was the opposite of what I experienced in the Falklands. 

Those two things - the loneliness of that freezing, empty island and the shock of seeing live video for the first time - ended up shaping my whole career.

It gave me a real drive for new tech that changes how companies work. It also made me realise the tools we build aren't just about saving money or making people work faster - they're for people. Whether that's employees trying to do their jobs, or families separated by thousands of miles of ocean who just want to feel closer.

Since those early days, the whole sector has changed completely. We used to rely on massive, expensive kit stuck inside dedicated boardrooms. Now, everything just runs as simple software on our laptops or mobile phones. We stopped messing about with separate networks and bundled everything together. You don't even have to book meetings days in advance anymore either; you just hop onto a quick, casual chat whenever you need to.

It's funny, looking back - we went from constantly asking if people could actually hear us to just saying, "I'll send over a link."

Jump on a call

But the real win with all this change is how easy it's made everything to use. Nowadays, pretty much anyone can jump onto a video call from wherever they happen to be.

Working from home is normal life now, and teams are scattered all over the place. It’s also made it way easier to keep in touch with people, whether that’s colleagues or family overseas. It’s still a bit mind-boggling that all the kit which used to fill massive metal racks now slides right into your pocket.

When I think about it, my job has never really been about the technology itself. It’s always been about people. It's about stopping all the little frustrations that get in the way when we try to talk to each other, and making the world feel a bit smaller when people are miles apart. Mostly, I just wanted to make sure nobody else had to feel as completely cut off as I did during that Christmas down in the Falklands.

The move to unified communications didn't just shake up the tech sector, it’s completely changed everyone’s lives. Even now, it’s still altering the way we get through our workdays, whether in a global pandemic or a heatwave in the UK. And, more importantly, keeping in touch with each other.

Tim Banting has been a technology analyst for over 12 years and has worked in IT for nearly 30 years. He is currently founder and principal analyst at So What? Now What?

title: Government gives regulatory boost to support AI in legal sector
raw_text:
The UK government has opened up applications for its new Legal Services AI Growth Lab, which aims to help law firms, conveyancers and legal technology companies adopt artificial intelligence (AI) faster.

The previous Keir Starmer administration unveiled its AI Growth Lab plan in 2025, with the aim of supporting growth and responsible AI innovation by making targeted regulatory modifications under robust safeguards and with careful monitoring. 

The government sees the legal sector as one that will benefit from greater use of AI if regulations can be tweaked to enable the use of the technology for document processing and analysis. When it opened up a consultation on its AI Growth Lab proposal, the government said AI could support complex elements of the planning process such as environmental impact assessments, where machine learning and large language models could reduce the burden of assessment and help decision-makers and communities make best use of the documents that need to be analysed.

Legal firms taking part in the Legal Services AI Growth Lab will be able to work directly with regulators to understand how existing rules apply to AI, identify barriers slowing adoption and get practical support on using the technology responsibly.

The UK’s AI minister, Kanishka Narayan, said: “The legal services sector employs over 317,000 people up and down the country, and it’s a fundamental part of how we do business and access justice. Society and the economy simply don’t work without it.

“In many ways, this sector is the exemplar case for just how impactful AI is set to be. Smart, responsible use of this technology could make legal services radically more accessible and free up legal professionals to focus on the complex, high-value work where human judgement is irreplaceable. But to make that happen, it’s critical that we get the regulation right, and this first AI Growth Lab will guide us all as we start that important journey.”

The lab brings together the Council for Licensed Conveyancers, the Solicitors Regulation Authority, the Information Commissioner’s Office and the Legal Services Board, with a view to identifying regulatory barriers to the roll-out of AI in legal services.

AI has the potential to make legal services faster, more affordable and easier to access, such as streamlining solicitors’ work, which, if the savings are passed on, means small businesses will face lower legal fees when they need to recover unpaid debts through the courts. Another example of AI efficiency gains is in the property buying and selling process, where AI systems could be used to analyse documents and free up conveyancers to focus on more complex tasks. 

Commenting on the scope for using AI in legal services, justice minister Sarah Sackman KC said: “The legal sector is one of the UK’s greatest economic strengths, generating more than £40bn in recent years. It is important that our services industry keeps pace and remains at the forefront of digital innovation. 

“That is why we are accelerating innovation across the legal sector, boosting productivity and delivering a modern justice system that can help cement the UK’s position as a global leader in legal services.”
